title: Tahdig
subtitle: crispy-bottomed Persian rice
excerpt: Tahdig is the crown jewel of Persian cooking: a pot of steamed rice with a golden, shatteringly crisp crust at the bottom. Every grain on top is separate and fluffy. Serves 4.
sourceNotes: Tahdig is one of the most technically demanding preparations in Persian cooking and a point of pride in every household. The technique of double-cooking rice with a steam trap is unique to Iran.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Soak the rice up to 24 hours ahead. Do not cook ahead as the crust softens on standing.

glossaryTerms.definition: Literally 'bottom of the pot' in Persian, the golden, crispy crust that forms at the base of the rice during the second stage of cooking.
Resting rice in salted water before cooking to hydrate the grains, shorten cooking time and improve texture.

content.text: is cooked in two stages: a brief boil followed by a long, low steam.
the rice first is essential. It hydrates the grains so they cook through during the steam without becoming waterlogged. Serves 4.
The yoghurt in the base creates a layer that insulates and bronzes the crust. The result is a golden disk that is unmoulded at the table. Getting the crust to release cleanly is the skill.

Soak the rinsed rice in cold water for 30 minutes. Drain. Bring the 2 litres of generously salted water to a rolling boil. Add the drained rice and boil for exactly 6 minutes. The rice should be cooked on the outside but still have a slight bite in the centre. Drain through the sieve.
In a small bowl, mix the yoghurt with half the melted butter, half the saffron water and 2 large spoonfuls of the parboiled rice. Stir to combine. This is the crust mixture.
Heat the oil and remaining butter in the saucepan over medium heat. Spread the yoghurt-rice mixture evenly across the base of the pan. Pack it down gently with the back of a spoon.

Mound the remaining rice on top of the crust base. Use the handle of a wooden spoon to poke 5 holes through the rice to the base. This lets steam escape. Drizzle the remaining saffron water over the top. Wrap the pan lid in a clean tea towel, tie the towel above the lid so it doesn't touch the rice, then cover the pan tightly.

Cook over medium heat for 5 minutes until you see steam rising. Reduce to very low heat and cook for a further 40 minutes. Remove from the heat and rest with the lid on for 5 minutes. Place a large plate over the pan and invert in one swift motion. The golden crust should come away cleanly.

attrs.problem: Crust won't release from the pan
attrs.solution: Immediately after inverting, place the pan with a damp cloth on the base for 2 minutes. The steam and cold will help loosen the crust. If it still sticks, ease around the edges with a spatula.

attrs.problem: Rice is soggy rather than fluffy
attrs.solution: The parboiling time or the soaking step may have been too long. The grains need to be just barely undercooked at the boiling stage. The steam phase finishes them through.
The heat was too high during the steam phase. Use the lowest possible heat setting on your hob. A heat diffuser is helpful if your lowest setting is still too strong.

content.text: Tahdig is not a side dish in Iran. It is the goal of cooking rice. Every guest at a Persian table expects a piece of the golden crust. The cook is judged by how evenly it browns. Some families use potato slices or flatbread instead of the yoghurt base. The double-steam technique is specific to Iran and not found in the rice traditions of neighbouring countries.
